rv.q: The play is helped by two stunning performances - by Turner, who pretty much never leaves the stage, and Evan Jonigkeit, making his Broadway debut as the addict Cody. Watching these two angry, broken, world-weary animals circle each other is an uncomfortable pleasure...[Turner] is the play's fairy godmother and soul.
It's more convincing as an actor's vehicle than as a play, an imbalance that Rob Ruggiero's pedestrian production fails to correct.
The musical 'High,' which opened on Tuesday night at the Booth Theater, is a well-intentioned but ultimately earthbound effort to dramatize the struggles of addiction and recovery.
To be remotely bearable, the ham-fisted melodrama 'High' requires a larger-than-life icon who can sink her teeth into its ripe dialogue.

Turner, who branded herself on Broadway as Tennessee Williams' Maggie the Cat and as Edward Albee's Martha the Viper, wouldn't seem an immediate casting choice to play a nun -- even a tough-talking modern one with street clothes and her own damaged history of bad boys and booze.
Turner does her best to bring warmth and intelligence to the brass-knuckled nun, but this troubled saint remains a flimsy character in a hollow play.
But if you grew up watching Bugs Bunny and "The Wizard of Oz" instead of Nickelodeon and "High School Musical," then you'll likely find "Wonderland" to be too namby-pamby for words.
Even if High didn’t have such stiff competition, it would still come across as sub-Lifetime-movie stuff.
It's shameful that High never manages to dig any deeper in that moment or any moment.
Alas, for the most part, High gave me a crisis of my own.
Nevertheless, the play comes off as a dull three-character mystery that pales in comparison with more compelling thrillers such as "Equus" and "Agnes of God."
